A 7‑day celery/cucumber juice cleanse is **not a safe or proven replacement for gout medication**. These juices are low in purines, and extra fluids may help hydration, but they do not reliably lower uric acid or treat the inflammation of a flare. Cleanses can cause inadequate calories/protein, electrolyte problems, blood-sugar changes, and dehydration—especially if you have kidney disease, diabetes, or take diuretics. Avoid adding lots of fruit juice or sweeteners, since fructose can worsen gout.

Apple cider vinegar has no good evidence for preventing or treating gout. It may irritate the stomach/esophagus, damage teeth, lower potassium, and interact with insulin, diuretics, or some other medicines. During a flare, use the treatment recommended by your clinician (often an NSAID, colchicine, or steroid); continue prescribed urate-lowering medicine such as allopurinol unless told otherwise. Hydrate, avoid alcohol—especially beer—and limit sugary drinks and organ/red meats. Seek urgent care for fever, a very hot/red joint, severe illness, or a first-ever attack, as infection can look like gout.

Causes can include pneumonia, tuberculosis, COVID, or other lung conditions; you may need a chest X‑ray and infection testing. Until evaluated, wear a well-fitting mask around others, improve ventilation, and avoid close contact, especially with children or immunocompromised people.

For temporary relief, try warm fluids or 1–2 teaspoons of honey (if age >1), and consider guaifenesin for mucus or dextromethorphan for a dry cough, following package directions and checking with a pharmacist if you take other medicines. In Australia, you’d usually wait until at least **6 months after your last COVID-19 vaccine dose** (or confirmed infection) before another dose. At 5 months, waiting about another month is generally appropriate unless a clinician recommends an earlier dose because of an outbreak, travel, or significant immune suppression.

ATAGI advice depends on age and risk: adults **75+** are generally eligible every 6 months; those **65–74**, and younger adults with severe immunocompromise or major risk factors, may be advised annual or sometimes 6‑monthly doses after individual assessment. Healthy younger adults may only need an annual dose or may not be routinely advised another one. Because recommendations are updated, check the current Australian Immunisation Handbook/Health Department guidance or ask your GP/pharmacist, particularly if you’re immunocompromised, pregnant, or recently had COVID-19.

Dear Colleague, please evaluate this 28-year-old patient for postpartum telogen effluvium. Diffuse shedding typically begins 2–4 months after delivery, peaks around month 4, and resolves spontaneously within 6–12 months, often by the child’s first birthday. Please assess for focal loss, scalp inflammation, scarring, or androgen excess. Suggested initial testing includes CBC, ferritin with iron studies, and TSH (± free T4). Consider vitamin D, B12, zinc, CMP, or androgen studies only when dietary risk, malabsorption, systemic symptoms, menstrual irregularity, or hyperandrogenism is present.

Management is primarily reassurance, adequate protein/caloric intake, gentle hair care, and correction of confirmed iron, thyroid, or nutritional abnormalities. Routine biotin or “hair vitamins” are not proven beneficial; biotin can also interfere with laboratory assays. Topical minoxidil may help persistent/chronic shedding, but postpartum use—especially during breastfeeding—should be individualized after discussing limited lactation safety data. Dermatology referral is appropriate for focal/scarring loss, diagnostic uncertainty, or shedding persisting beyond 12 months.

No. There is currently **no solid clinical evidence** that transdermal magnesium—such as magnesium oils, sprays, creams, or Epsom-salt baths—meaningfully raises magnesium levels or relieves fibromyalgia pain. Human studies are small, poorly controlled, or show inconsistent skin absorption, and major fibromyalgia guidelines do not recommend it. Evidence for oral magnesium in fibromyalgia is also limited, although correcting a confirmed magnesium deficiency is appropriate.

Topical magnesium may feel soothing because of massage, warmth, or relaxation, but it can cause skin irritation and should not replace evidence-based care. Better-supported approaches include graded aerobic/strength exercise, sleep and stress management, cognitive behavioral therapy, and—when suitable—medicines such as duloxetine, milnacipran, pregabalin, or low-dose amitriptyline. If you try topical magnesium, view it as an optional comfort measure rather than a proven treatment.

Daily cranberry capsules do **not definitely prevent** urinary tract infections (UTIs). The best available evidence, including a 2023 Cochrane review of 50 randomized trials, found that cranberry products probably modestly reduce symptomatic, laboratory-confirmed UTIs in women with recurrent infections, children, and some people at increased risk after urinary procedures. However, benefits were not clearly demonstrated in older institutionalized adults, pregnant women, or people with bladder-emptying problems.

Evidence specifically for capsules is less certain because products contain widely varying amounts of proanthocyanidins—the proposed active compounds—and optimal dose and duration remain unclear. Cranberry may be a reasonable low-risk preventive option for recurrent UTIs, but it is not guaranteed and should not replace prescribed prevention or antibiotic treatment for an active infection. Side effects can include stomach upset; people taking warfarin should seek medical advice because of a possible interaction.

Wash with soap and water, use a cold compress, avoid scratching, and consider an oral antihistamine for itching if you can safely take one. You can outline the redness with a pen and note the time to see whether it spreads.

Seek medical care promptly if redness keeps expanding, pain/warmth/swelling worsens after 24–48 hours, pus or drainage appears, red streaks travel up the limb, nearby glands swell, or you develop fever, chills, marked fatigue, or feel ill. Get urgent help now for trouble breathing, facial/tongue swelling, faintness, widespread hives, severe pain, rapidly spreading redness, or skin turning dark/blistered. If a tick may have been attached, contact a clinician for an enlarging rash (often larger than 2 inches/5 cm and not always bull’s-eye shaped), fever, headache, body aches, or joint pain. Ensure your tetanus vaccination is current, particularly if the skin was broken.

Malaria is possible if you live in or recently visited a malaria area, but these symptoms also occur with dengue, flu/COVID, typhoid, and other infections. A rapid diagnostic “dip” test is usually appropriate and can confirm many malaria cases, but it is not perfect: early infection, low parasite levels, or some parasite strains can cause a false negative, while some tests remain positive after a past infection. Get tested at the health center today. If the first test is negative but fever continues or suspicion is high, you need reassessment and often repeat testing within 12–24 hours or referral for microscopy.

Do not start antimalarial medicine on your own—the correct treatment depends on the test result, local drug resistance, malaria species, pregnancy, age, and illness severity. Drink fluids and use acetaminophen/paracetamol as directed; avoid aspirin or ibuprofen until dengue is excluded. Seek emergency care now for confusion, fainting, breathing difficulty, seizures, severe weakness, repeated vomiting, inability to drink, jaundice, very dark urine, bleeding, or worsening severe abdominal pain.

Current evidence does not support routine FMT capsules for moderate ulcerative colitis. Several small randomized studies and meta-analyses suggest a modest induction benefit in selected patients, but results are heterogeneous across donor selection, dosing, pretreatment, route, and concomitant therapy. Durable remission and maintenance efficacy remain uncertain because follow-up is generally short; favorable case reports cannot resolve this. Major gastroenterology guidelines generally restrict FMT for UC to clinical trials, unlike its established role in recurrent *C. difficile* infection.

Short-term adverse events are often mild GI symptoms, but uncommon serious events—including bacteremia and transmission of multidrug-resistant or enteric organisms—have occurred. Capsules do not eliminate these risks, and long-term metabolic, immune, and microbiome consequences are unknown. I would therefore not offer capsule FMT as standard care or in place of proven UC therapies. If considered, it should preferably be within an IRB-approved trial using rigorously screened, traceable donor material, current pathogen-screening standards, explicit consent about uncertain durability and infectious risk, and structured safety/long-term follow-up. Overall: promising, but too early for routine recommendation.

This sounds like motion sickness. For your trip, sit in the front passenger seat and look straight ahead at the horizon; avoid reading, scrolling, or watching videos. Keep cool air flowing, minimize strong smells, and keep your head supported and as still as possible. Before leaving, eat a small bland meal rather than traveling with an empty or very full stomach; avoid greasy/spicy foods, alcohol, and excess caffeine. Sip water, take regular fresh-air breaks, and prioritize a good night’s sleep. Ginger tea/candies or acupressure wristbands help some people, though evidence is mixed.

If possible, travel during a time when you can rest, and stop promptly if you feel close to vomiting—don’t drive while significantly nauseated or distracted. Seek medical advice if this is new or worsening, occurs without travel, or comes with severe headache, fainting, hearing changes, weakness, chest pain, or persistent vomiting/dehydration.

This is **treatment of active HSV**, not prophylaxis. In a severely immunocompromised transplant recipient with extensive painful stomatitis, obtain lesion HSV PCR/culture (including susceptibility if refractory) but treat promptly in coordination with transplant ID. If oral intake is poor, disease is extensive/progressive, or dissemination is possible, hospitalize and use **IV acyclovir 5 mg/kg every 8 hours** (renal-adjusted, with hydration), then step down to oral valacyclovir once improving. Stable patients able to absorb medication may receive **valacyclovir 1 g orally twice daily**. Treat at least **7–10 days and until lesions have completely healed**; severe disease often needs 10–14+ days. Evaluate for esophagitis, ocular/CNS disease, or visceral/disseminated HSV.

Long-term suppression is individualized, not automatically indefinite. **Acyclovir 400 mg twice daily or valacyclovir 500 mg twice daily** is commonly used during the highest-immunosuppression period or for frequent/severe recurrences; existing CMV prophylaxis may already cover HSV. Reassess as immunosuppression decreases. Lack of improvement after 5–7 days raises concern for acyclovir resistance and warrants ID-guided testing and alternatives such as foscarnet.

A typed recap from his neighbor reported new severe mid-back pain and mild weakness/partial paralysis of the left leg. Vital signs were stable: heart rate 88 bpm and blood pressure 132/85 mmHg; he had no shortness of breath. Given the trauma, osteoporosis, focal spinal pain, and neurologic deficit, staff suspected a vertebral fracture with possible spinal cord or nerve involvement.

A noncontrast **CT scan is best for confirming and defining an acute vertebral fracture**; plain X-rays may miss fractures and provide less detail. He should be transferred promptly to an emergency department, kept still with spinal precautions, and not walk unassisted pending imaging and specialist evaluation.

They can be triggered by reflux, medications, alcohol, or irritation of the diaphragm, but occasionally signal a lung, heart, brain, kidney, or metabolic problem. Go to urgent care/ER now if you also have chest pain, trouble breathing, severe headache, weakness/numbness, confusion, fever, repeated vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, or cannot sleep/eat/drink.

Eat small meals and avoid alcohol, carbonated drinks, spicy foods, and rapid eating. Don’t use risky remedies such as choking yourself or swallowing large amounts of sugar. A clinician may check medications and underlying causes and prescribe treatments such as baclofen, metoclopramide, or chlorpromazine if appropriate.

In a 7-year-old, clinicians should document the bruises carefully, obtain a history separately from the child and caregivers using neutral questions, assess for other injuries, and consider bleeding disorders or accidental causes. Testing may include a blood count and clotting studies, with imaging guided by symptoms and examination.

Two syncopal episodes in one week warrant prompt in-person evaluation rather than assuming dehydration. Start with detailed history/witness account (during exertion or supine, prodrome, palpitations, bleeding, medications/substances, family history of sudden death), full cardiac/neurologic exam, orthostatic vitals, and a 12-lead ECG. Check pregnancy status and glucose; CBC/electrolytes are reasonable when suggested by bleeding, volume loss, or other clinical findings. Routine head CT, EEG, carotid imaging, or broad lab panels generally have low yield without focal neurologic signs, seizure features, trauma, or a specific indication.

Send her to the ED now for exertional or supine syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, abnormal ECG, significant injury, persistent symptoms, neurologic deficits, active bleeding, or family history of sudden unexplained death. At present, there is **no robust evidence that newer peptide-based vaccines prolong overall survival in metastatic cutaneous melanoma**. Most personalized neoantigen or multipeptide vaccines have only phase I/early phase II data: small, often single-arm cohorts showing feasibility, immunogenicity, and occasional durable responses—frequently alongside checkpoint inhibitors—but not randomized, adequately powered survival benefit. Any apparent OS signal is highly vulnerable to selection and combination-treatment effects.

Older gp100 peptide-vaccine trials were mixed; one randomized study with high-dose IL-2 improved response rate and progression-free survival, but the OS difference was not statistically significant. Also, tebentafusp has proven an OS benefit in metastatic uveal melanoma, but it is a gp100-directed T-cell receptor fusion drug, **not a vaccine**, and should not be extrapolated to peptide vaccination. Clinically, these vaccines remain investigational unless a specific product has mature randomized phase III OS data; the key evidence to seek is an active-control trial with prespecified OS, sufficient follow-up, and results separable from checkpoint blockade.

They do not treat typical osteoarthritis. Vitamins and minerals are both micronutrients your body needs in small amounts, but they’re different substances. **Vitamins** are organic compounds made by plants or animals and can sometimes be broken down by heat, light, or storage. Examples include vitamin C (supports immunity and wound healing), vitamin D (helps absorb calcium and supports bones), and B vitamins (help turn food into energy).

**Minerals** are inorganic elements that come from soil and water and generally remain stable during cooking. Examples include calcium (bones and teeth), iron (helps blood carry oxygen), magnesium (supports muscles and nerves), and potassium (helps regulate fluid balance and heart function). A varied diet—fruits, vegetables, whole grains, dairy or fortified alternatives, protein foods, nuts, and seeds—usually provides both. Supplements can help with specific gaps, but more isn’t always better, so check with a healthcare professional before taking high doses, especially during pregnancy or while using medications.

Other urgent signs include trouble breathing, wheezing/stridor, hoarse voice, tongue or lip swelling, dizziness, fainting, confusion, weak rapid pulse, vomiting, or rapidly worsening symptoms.

Give **intramuscular epinephrine immediately** in the outer mid-thigh (use the prescribed autoinjector), call emergency services, and do not leave the patient alone. Unexplained bruising can come from many causes, and it isn’t possible to tell which one you have from bruises alone. Inherited conditions include von Willebrand disease and, less commonly, hemophilia—especially with a family history, prolonged bleeding after dental work or surgery, frequent nosebleeds, heavy periods, or deep muscle/joint bleeding. Other possibilities include low or poorly functioning platelets, liver disease, vitamin deficiencies, fragile skin, or medicines/supplements such as aspirin, ibuprofen, anticoagulants, steroids, fish oil, or ginkgo.

Normal basic tests do not exclude every bleeding disorder. Seek urgent care for rapidly spreading bruising, pinpoint red spots, bleeding that won’t stop, blood in urine/stool, severe headache, weakness, dizziness, or unusually heavy menstrual bleeding. Type 1 diabetes requires lifelong insulin, ideally started and adjusted with an endocrinology/diabetes team. Most people use a basal–bolus plan: long-acting insulin once or twice daily plus rapid-acting insulin before meals, or an insulin pump. Doses depend on weight, carbohydrate intake, activity, illness, and glucose patterns—do not change them without a personalized plan. Learn carbohydrate counting, correction dosing, injection-site rotation, and glucose monitoring; a continuous glucose monitor is often helpful. During the early “honeymoon” phase, needs may temporarily fall, but insulin should not be stopped.

Know hypoglycemia signs (shaking, sweating, confusion): take 15 g fast carbohydrate, recheck after 15 minutes, and repeat if still low. Keep glucagon available and teach household members to use it. Check ketones when ill or glucose is persistently ≥250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L), stay hydrated, and never omit basal insulin during illness. Seek emergency care for vomiting, abdominal pain, deep/rapid breathing, marked drowsiness, or moderate/large ketones, as these may indicate diabetic ketoacidosis. Arrange prompt diabetes education and follow-up for individualized targets and dosing.

The **YEARS algorithm** is used to rule out pulmonary embolism (PE) in a clinically stable patient with suspected PE. Assess 3 items: signs of DVT, hemoptysis, and “PE is the most likely diagnosis.” If **none** are present, PE can generally be excluded with a **D-dimer <1,000 ng/mL FEU**; if **one or more** are present, use **<500 ng/mL FEU**. Above the applicable threshold usually prompts CT pulmonary angiography (or V/Q scanning when appropriate). YEARS should be applied within a validated local pathway—not when the patient is unstable or PE probability is already very high.

**Wells** uses more variables and weighted points (DVT signs, PE more likely than alternatives, heart rate >100, recent surgery/immobilization, prior PE/DVT, hemoptysis, malignancy) to classify pretest probability. Low/unlikely risk may first undergo PERC or D-dimer testing; high/likely risk generally proceeds to imaging. New/worsening breathlessness, chest pain, fainting, coughing blood, low oxygen, or unilateral leg swelling warrants urgent assessment.

WHO separately addresses chronic draining ears with ear cleaning and topical quinolone drops rather than routine oral antibiotics. A neurological disease in one cousin does not necessarily mean it is inherited. Many neurological conditions are acquired or occur sporadically, and risk depends heavily on the exact diagnosis, age at onset, and whether other relatives—especially your father, siblings, grandparents, aunts, or uncles—have similar problems. Even inherited conditions can have different inheritance patterns and may not significantly raise your risk.

Try to obtain your cousin’s confirmed diagnosis and, if available, any genetic test result. Write down affected relatives, their relationship to you, symptoms, and age at diagnosis, then discuss this with your primary-care clinician or a genetic counselor. Genetic testing is most informative when it begins with the affected person and should not be ordered without counseling, since results may be uncertain. If you currently have new weakness, loss of coordination, seizures, confusion, severe sudden headache, or speech/vision changes, seek urgent medical care.

An itchy throat and neck rash soon after eating may indicate a food allergy, which can become more severe without warning. Stop eating the suspected food and avoid it until you’re evaluated. If you have trouble breathing, throat/tongue swelling, hoarseness, wheezing, dizziness/fainting, repeated vomiting, or rapidly spreading hives, call emergency services immediately; if you have an epinephrine auto-injector, use it promptly. Don’t rely on antihistamines for breathing or throat symptoms.

Arrange an appointment soon with an allergist or clinician. Record what you ate, ingredients, timing, symptoms, medications, and take photos of the rash; save packaging or restaurant ingredient information if possible. Don’t deliberately test the food at home. For mild skin symptoms only, an over-the-counter non-drowsy antihistamine may help if it’s safe for you, but ask a pharmacist or clinician about the right product and whether you need an epinephrine prescription and emergency action plan.

Lying down can trigger reflux or musculoskeletal discomfort, but chest pressure can also represent heart-related disease, a blood clot, or another serious condition—even if symptoms are intermittent or mild.

If the pressure is happening now, lasts more than 5–10 minutes, recurs, or comes with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness, fainting, palpitations, or pain spreading to the arm, jaw, back, or shoulder, **call emergency services now and do not drive yourself**. The threshold should be especially low with heart/lung disease, diabetes, smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, pregnancy/postpartum status, or older age. If symptoms have stopped and none of those warning signs occurred, you should still have prompt same-day medical assessment; an exam, ECG, and sometimes blood tests are needed to safely distinguish reflux from heart or lung causes.

Yunnan does not require a different “local” regimen; standard altitude guidance applies. Risk depends on itinerary: Kunming (~1,900 m), Dali (~2,000 m), and Lijiang (~2,400 m) usually need no medication. Rapid travel to sleep in Shangri-La (~3,200 m), especially during a 5-day trip or with prior altitude illness, makes prophylaxis reasonable. Jade Dragon Snow Mountain reaches >4,500 m; a brief visit can still cause symptoms, though sleeping altitude matters most. Avoid same-day ascent from low altitude to >3,000 m if possible, limit alcohol/exertion initially, hydrate normally, and do not rely on canned oxygen or herbal products.

Typical prophylaxis is acetazolamide 125 mg twice daily, starting the day before ascent and continuing for 48 hours after reaching the highest sleeping altitude (longer if still ascending). Dexamethasone is an alternative when acetazolamide cannot be used but requires clinician guidance. Headache plus nausea, dizziness, fatigue, or poor sleep suggests acute mountain sickness; stop ascending. Confusion, inability to walk straight, or breathlessness at rest requires immediate descent and emergency care.

New inability to grip or lift a cup with one hand may be a **stroke or other neurologic emergency**, even without pain. Note the exact time they were last known normal and call emergency medical services now. Check for facial droop, slurred/confused speech, new arm or leg weakness/numbness, vision change, severe dizziness, or sudden severe headache—but do not delay the call. If available, check glucose and vital signs while EMS is coming.

Keep them seated or lying safely, monitor breathing, and do not give food, drink, aspirin, or medications because swallowing may be impaired and some strokes involve bleeding. Do not drive them yourself. Have their medication list, allergies, diagnoses, anticoagulant use, and baseline function ready for EMS.

Ask your oncologist for the therapy’s response rate, typical duration of benefit, survival improvement, and results specifically for patients like you.
